messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 37
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: North American
- Relationship Status: Divorced
- Occupation: Database Administrator
- Trauma Type: Life-threatening illness
- Pcl5: 48

He is 37 and works as a database administrator, a job that fits him in the ways he has always preferred: structured, precise, mostly quiet, with clear systems that can be checked and corrected when something goes wrong. Before the illness, he describes himself as someone who relied on logic and routines, the kind of man who kept backup plans for his backup plans. He is divorced now, and he speaks about that part of his life with a muted kind of regret, as if it belongs to a version of himself that still believed there would always be more time.

The traumatic event begins with what he first assumes is a stomach bug. He notices a strange fatigue, then a dull ache that will not settle. He keeps working, telling himself he is being dramatic. When the pain worsens and he starts to run a fever, he finally goes to urgent care, expecting antibiotics and a quick return to normal. Instead, the situation escalates quickly. He is sent to the hospital, then kept for tests, then told that something serious is happening inside his body. He remembers the atmosphere more than the words: the fluorescent lights, the clipped voices, the way his phone feels heavy in his hand as he tries to explain to his ex-wife why he needs help. Within days, he is facing a life-threatening illness that seems to strip away the steadiness he has built his life around. He says the most frightening part was not only the fear of dying, but the sense that his body had become unreliable without warning.

During the acute medical crisis, he moves through the hospital in a fog of pain, medications, and fear. He becomes hyperaware of every sensation: a twinge in his abdomen, a spike in his temperature, the sound of footsteps in the hallway. He watches the monitors as if they are the only honest thing in the room. He starts to anticipate catastrophe from the smallest changes in his body. If a nurse looks concerned, he assumes the worst. If a doctor is delayed, he imagines bad news. He feels trapped by the waiting, helpless in a way that is profoundly unfamiliar to him. Later, when he tries to describe that time, he returns again and again to the image of lying still while other people made decisions about whether he would live.

He survives, but recovery is not the clean relief he expected. At first he tries to be grateful and practical, focusing on follow-up appointments, lab results, and medication schedules. He returns to work because it feels like one of the few places where he can still identify patterns and control outcomes. But even at his desk, he finds himself scanning his body instead of his screen. A dull ache or a wave of nausea can pull him out of meetings. He refreshes medical portals repeatedly, searching for certainty in numbers he does not fully trust. He becomes preoccupied with illness in a way he never was before, checking his temperature, his skin, his appetite, his energy, as though vigilance might prevent a repeat of what happened.

He is also more easily startled than he used to be. A call from an unknown number, a message from a doctor’s office, the sound of a hospital television in a waiting room can send a jolt through him. Nights are difficult. He falls asleep tired and wakes up alert, sometimes with a rush of panic he cannot immediately place. He dreams of being back in the hospital, unable to get anyone’s attention, trying to speak but not being able to make himself understood. In the morning, he often lies still for a few minutes, listening to his own breathing to make sure it sounds normal.

His divorce now feels connected to the illness in ways he does not say directly at first. He and his ex-wife had already been under strain, but the hospitalization makes his dependency visible, and he feels ashamed of needing help. He notices how quickly he becomes withdrawn when he feels unwell, how hard it is for him to let someone see his fear. He says he became “hard to be around” afterward, more irritable, more guarded, less willing to talk about what he was experiencing. There is a loss not just of health, but of the version of himself who assumed his body would obey him and that life could be managed through competence alone.

Now he lives with a constant expectation that something may be missed. He still functions well at work, often impressively so, but it takes more effort than others can see. He triple-checks systems, documents everything, and finds himself drawn to tasks that have a beginning, middle, and end because they offer a kind of closure he cannot find in his own body. He wants to move forward, but part of him remains on alert, waiting for the next sign that the threat is returning.
